clips.send: Zhang Qian. Western Han, 138–126 BC. Emperor Wu of Han sent him to find the Yuezhi people and team up against the Xiongnu. Captured by the Xiongnu and held for more than 10 years. Deserts and the high Pamir mountains. Captured again on the way home. First-hand knowledge of the Western Regions (西域). News of Dayuan’s fine “heavenly horses”. Later: grapes, alfalfa, pomegranates, walnuts reach China. His journeys strengthened ties between the Central Plains and the Western Regions; the Silk Road took shape. In 60 BC the Western Han set up the Protectorate of the Western Regions — today’s Xinjiang formally came under the central government.

clips.send: Zheng He. Ming, 1405–1433. The Yongle Emperor sent him to the “Western Oceans” to strengthen ties with overseas countries. Storms and typhoons at sea. Timing the monsoon winds right. Pirates near Palembang (旧港). Finding the way across open ocean. A giraffe — welcomed as a “qilin” (麒麟). Spices, gems and envoys from many lands. Took out: silk, porcelain, tea and iron goods. Seven voyages (1405–1433) reached more than 30 countries and regions in Asia and Africa — as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea — decades before Europe’s great voyages.

clips.send: Xuanzang. Tang, 629–645 (some say 627). A young monk who wanted to study Buddhism where it began, in Tianzhu (天竺, ancient India). Slipped out past Tang border guards (travel was banned). Lost his water in the Mohe-yan desert: 4 nights and 5 days without a drop. An icy pass over the Tian Shan. Thousands of km of mountains on the way home. 657 Buddhist books (traditional figure). Translated over 1,300 scrolls with his team. Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (《大唐西域记》). His book, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, describes over 100 lands. It is still a key source for the history of Central Asia and India.

clips.send: Jianzhen. Tang, 742–754. Japanese monks invited this famous teacher from Yangzhou to bring Buddhist rules to Japan. Attempt 1: plans reported to officials — stopped. Attempts 2–3: ships wrecked by storms. Attempt 4: stopped by officials. Attempt 5: blown 14 days south to Hainan; he goes blind. Attempt 6: success! Buddhist rules (precepts) for Japan. Tang architecture: Tōshōdai-ji temple (唐招提寺). Medicine, calligraphy and sculpture. After six attempts and going blind, he reached Japan in 754 (some say 753). He made an important contribution to cultural exchange between China and Japan.

clips.send: Marco Polo. Yuan, 1271–1295. A young merchant from Venice who travelled with his father and uncle to the court of Kublai Khan. Deserts and the high, cold Pamirs. A long illness on the way (about a year). A dangerous two-year sea voyage home. The Travels of Marco Polo (《马可·波罗行纪》). Tales of Dadu (Beijing), paper money and post stations. Europe’s curiosity about the East. His book describes the wealth of Yuan China and the splendour of Dadu, and made many Europeans eager to reach the East. (Some scholars doubt parts of his story.)

clips.send: 张骞。西汉 · 前138—前126年。汉武帝派他联络大月氏，共同夹击匈奴。被匈奴扣留十多年。沙漠和高耸的葱岭。回程途中再次被匈奴扣留。对西域各国的第一手了解。大宛“汗血马”的消息。后来：葡萄、苜蓿、石榴、核桃等传入中原。张骞通西域，加强了中原和西域的联系，丝绸之路由此形成。公元前60年，西汉设立西域都护，今新疆地区正式归属中央政权。

clips.send: 马可·波罗。元 · 1271—1295年。一位威尼斯青年商人，随父亲和叔叔前往元世祖忽必烈的宫廷。沙漠和高寒的帕米尔高原。途中大病一场（约一年）。长达两年的艰险海路回国。《马可·波罗行纪》。关于大都、纸币和驿站的描述。欧洲人对东方的向往。《马可·波罗行纪》描述了元朝的富庶和大都的繁华，激起了欧洲人对东方的向往。（也有学者怀疑书中部分内容。）

clips.send: 玄奘。唐 · 629—645年（一说627年出发）。一位年轻僧人，想到佛教的发源地天竺（古印度）求取佛经。当时禁止私自出境，他偷偷越过边关。在莫贺延碛打翻水袋，四夜五日滴水未进。翻越天山冰雪覆盖的凌山。回程又要翻越葱岭等高山。佛经657部（传统说法）。与弟子译出佛经一千三百多卷。口述写成《大唐西域记》。《大唐西域记》记述了他亲历和听说的一百多个国家和地区，是研究中亚、印度等地历史的重要文献。

clips.send: 鉴真。唐 · 742—754年。日本僧人邀请扬州的高僧鉴真去日本传授佛教戒律。第一次：被人诬告，没能出发。第二、三次：船只遇风浪损坏。第四次：被官府拦回。第五次：漂流十四天到海南，双目失明。第六次：成功到达日本。佛教戒律传入日本。唐代建筑艺术：唐招提寺。医药、书法、雕塑。鉴真六次东渡，双目失明，终于在754年（一说753年）到达日本，为中日文化交流作出了重要贡献。

clips.send: 郑和。明 · 1405—1433年。明成祖派他出使“西洋”，加强与海外各国的联系。海上风暴和台风。必须算准季风时节。旧港一带的海盗。在茫茫大海上辨别方向。长颈鹿——被当作“麒麟”。香料、宝石和各国使节。带去：丝绸、瓷器、茶叶和铁器。郑和七次下西洋（1405—1433年），到达亚洲、非洲30多个国家和地区，最远到达非洲东海岸和红海沿岸，比欧洲航海家的远航早半个多世纪。
